```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(echarts4r)
library(vehicletrends)
library(palmerpenguins)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.path = "figs/",
  fig.width = 7.252,
  fig.height = 4,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.retina = 3
)

sp <- function(gap = 2, unit = "em") {
  sprintf('<div style="height: %s%s;"></div>', gap, unit)
}

rungbar <- function(n) {
  labs <- c(
    "a chart",
    "linked charts",
    "a box",
    "Shiny in the box",
    "anything in the box"
  )
  grp <- c("in", "in", "box", "box", "box")
  steps <- vapply(
    seq_along(labs),
    function(i) {
      sprintf(
        '<div class="rs rs-%s%s"><span class="rs-n">%d</span>%s</div>',
        grp[i],
        if (i == n) " is-on" else "",
        i,
        labs[i]
      )
    },
    character(1)
  )
  htmltools::HTML(paste0(
    '<div class="rungbar">',
    '<div class="rg rg-in">inside the document</div>',
    '<div class="rg rg-box">in a box</div>',
    paste(steps, collapse = ""),
    '</div>'
  ))
}
```

# I want [**these**]{.contentchip} sentences with [**this**]{.formatchip} layout

::: {.col .amberborder}
![](images/handwriting-practice-pokemon.png){fig-align="center" height="600"}
:::

::: {.col .blueborder}
![](images/handwriting-good-minecraft.png){fig-align="center" height="600"}
:::

::: {.notes}
Here's the problem with asking a model for a document.

I didn't want *a* handwriting sheet. I wanted **these words** in **this layout**.

Those are two different things — and when I ask for the finished document, I've
asked the model to generate both of them at the same time.
:::

{{< center >}}

# [Content]{.contentchip} entangled with [Format]{.formatchip}

{{< include svg/entanglement-1.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
What actually happened across those eight rounds?

Every time I re-prompted, I wasn't changing the thing I didn't like. I was
rolling the dice on the entire document again.

The model isn't editing a document. It's generating another document.

Don't say "LLMs are bad at formatting" — too easy to rebut. The argument is
that generation is probabilistic and rendering is deterministic.

Optional heading, if "entangled" feels like a word the audience has to accept
before the figure can work: **Every fix is a new document.** That is the actual
claim, and it needs no metaphor.
:::

---

{{< center >}}
{{< middle >}}

# Quarto disentangles [Content]{.contentchip .fragment .custom .turnsred data-fragment-index="3"} and [Format]{.formatchip}

{{< include svg/entanglement-2.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Define Quarto out loud here, about eight seconds: it's a plain-text
document — markdown with code in it — and `quarto render` turns it into a PDF,
or a website, or these slides.

The point isn't that the .qmd is prettier. It's that the weaving moved somewhere
I can reach, and reaching it took one step instead of eight.

Optional heading: **The weaving moves to render time.** Slightly more concrete
than "disentangles," and it sets up the next slide, which shows the seam.
:::

# [One `.qmd`, one folder of CSVs]{.center}

:::: {.col width="58%"}
[**`handwriting-practice.qmd`**]{.qmdblue .font120}

(written by Claude Code)

<br>

::: {.font70}
````{.markdown}
---
params:
  data_file: "data/minecraft.csv"
format: pdf
---

```{{r}}
sentences <- read.csv(params$data_file)$sentence
for (s in sentences) {
  cat(sprintf("\\practiceblock{%s}\n\n", s))
}
```
````
:::
::::

:::: {.col width="42%"}
[**`minecraft.csv`**]{.amber .font120}

(written by Me)

<br>

:::{.font70}
|sentence |
|-----|
|Minecraft is a popular building game.|
|Players mine for resources underground.|
|You can build almost anything you want.|
|Creepers are sneaky and dangerous enemies.|
|Diamonds are the best ore to find.|
|Players must survive through the first night.|
|The Nether is a hot and scary place.|
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Two files. The model wrote the left one, once. It has never seen the right one.

**Click 1 — the parameters.** The sentences aren't in the document. They're in a
file, and which file is an argument. That's what "the content has an address"
actually looks like on disk.

**Click 2 — the elision.** Those forty lines are TikZ: line heights, baselines,
the grey trace text the kid writes over. That is the format. I wrote it once and
I have not opened it since.

**Click 3 — the read.** One line. That's where the two halves meet, and it
happens at render, not in the model.

And because the file is parameterized, it isn't one worksheet — it's a worksheet
*generator*. A four-line loop renders every CSV in that folder into its own PDF.
Pokemon, minecraft, mario: same source.

Don't show `render.R`. Say "four lines" and move on; the loop is not the idea.

⚠️ Replace the CSV rows and the header with the real ones. This is the one slide
in the deck whose whole job is being a real file, so it must not stay a mock-up.

⚠️ Decide against the closing *change one word* slide (`format: pdf` →
`format: html`). Both slides change one thing in the YAML. Different claims —
many topics here, many formats there — but if they read as the same trick, the
second one deflates. Pick which gets the emphasis.
:::

# [[Ask for the [source]{.yellow},<br>not the [artifact]{.red}]{.font150}]{.center}

::: {.notes}
So here's the trick. Stop asking the model for the artifact.

Ask it for the source.
:::

---

{{< inverse >}}
{{< middle >}}

# [[Ask for the [~~source~~]{.yellow} [.qmd]{.yellow},<br>not the [artifact]{.red}]{.font150}]{.center}

::: {.notes}
And in Quarto, the source is a `.qmd`.

The agent writes the structure. Quarto takes responsibility for producing the
artifact.

See the next slide for an alternative to the strikethrough — use one or the
other, not both.
:::

---

{{< bg-color "#000000" >}}
{{< middle >}}
{{< center >}}

<br>
![](images/vehicletrends.gif){fig-align="center" width=100%}

::: {.notes}
A handwriting worksheet is a pretty trivial example. So why am I
talking about it at a session about dashboards?

Because a dashboard is just a document with a lot more that can go wrong: it has
layout, text, data, code, JavaScript, interaction. And I don't want a
model regenerating all of that every time I change one sentence.

I built this with Quarto.
:::

{{< center >}}
{{< middle >}}

{{< include svg/dashboard.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
This is the same picture from earlier, at site scale. Same me, same agent, same
`.qmd` — one of them is still literally the same box. Point at it; don't argue
the resemblance, the drawing is the argument.

At rest this is the picture from the very beginning of the talk: I asked for the
thing, and the agent handed me the thing. Only now the thing is a website.

Click 1 — but that's not what I asked for. I asked for the `.qmd`. Fifteen of
them. And notice where the arrow lands: on one page, not on the site.

Click 2: the data comes from outside. `library(vehicletrends)` runs during the
render, so the numbers get computed and baked in. The agent didn't write any of
them — it wrote one page.

Click 3: and I can still reach in. Prompt the agent to change a page, or open it
and change it myself. Same two arrows as three slides ago — that's the point,
they still work at fifteen pages.
:::

::: {.notes}
The agent pays for every character.

And it compounds over turns: about 81,000 tokens versus about 11,000 after ten
edits. The ratio never moves — the gap does.

The sharper version of the whole cost argument, worth saying out loud right
here: **it is not that markdown is smaller — it is that you stop paying for the
parts you did not change.** Character count is the proxy; regeneration is the
mechanism.
:::

# [Small pieces have small context windows]{.center}

::: {.col width="44%"}
<pre class="specimen treecard">
<span>vehicletrends.us/            lines</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── index.qmd                    7</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── about.qmd                  101</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── vmt-daily.qmd              216</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── vmt-age.qmd                351</span>
<span class="sp-hit">├── depreciation.qmd           324</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── percent-listings.qmd       620</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── percent-dealers.qmd        199</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── market-concentration.qmd   292</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── hhi-explained.qmd          331</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── registrations.qmd          349</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── nearest-vehicles.qmd        34</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── tech-stack.qmd              60</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── cite.qmd                    50</span>
<span class="sp-dim">├── LICENSE.qmd                 26</span>
<span class="sp-dim">└── 404.qmd                     21</span>
</pre>
:::

::: {.col width="56%"}
[**`depreciation.qmd`**]{.red .font120}

<pre class="specimen diffcard">
<span>  ## Depreciation by body style</span>
<span> </span>
<span>  Used trucks hold their value better</span>
<span class="sp-del">- than any other body style.</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ than any other body style, and the</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ gap has widened every year since 2022.</span>
</pre>
:::

::: {.notes}

And here's what I did **not** do: I did not regenerate the site. Nothing decided
the sidebar again, or the theme again, or the fourteen pages I never opened.
There is no version of this where the navigation quietly comes back different —
the same way there was no version of the worksheet where the layout drifted.

The numbers on those other pages aren't in these files either — that's
**`library(vehicletrends)`**, computed at render. Right now that just means the
agent doesn't have to write them. Later it means nobody can write the wrong one.
:::

## [To change one thing, what has to agree?]{.center}

<br>

::: {.col}
[**in an app**]{.red}

- the **input** that defines it
- the **output** that consumes it
- the **reactive** that connects them

[Three places, and they have to match.]{.font110}
:::

::: {.col}
[**in a page**]{.blue}

- the **chunk**

`r sp(1)`

[One place, and it's the one<br>I'm already looking at.]{.font110}
:::

<br>

[This isn't about how much you write. It's about how much has to be true at once —]{.font120}

[and *that* is what an agent has to hold in its head.]{.font130 .blue}

::: {.notes}
Here's the version of that which actually matters for an agent.

An application is a coupled thing, and it should be -- that coupling is what
makes it reactive. But it means adding one filter touches an input, an output,
and the reactive expression between them, and all three have to agree.

A page isn't coupled. Adding a filter is a chunk.

**The line to land:** this is not a claim about how much code you write. It's a
claim about how much has to be simultaneously true -- and that is exactly what
an agent has to hold in context to make a change safely.

Which is the same argument as the next slide, one level down. If you're running
that one too, this is the handoff: *"and it scales."*

Note there is no comparison of volume anywhere on this slide, and no number.
Nothing here says an app is worse. It says an app is *coupled*, which is what
an app is for.
:::

# [Quarto is checkable twice]{.center}

<br>

::: {.col .fragment}
## [**By machine**]{.darkgreen}

### `quarto render` is a compile step

<pre class="specimen errcard">
<span class="sp-dim">Quitting from index.qmd:12-30 [africa-map]</span>
<span class="sp-err">Error:</span>
<span class="sp-err">! all(funding$name %in% africa$name) is not TRUE</span>
<span>Execution halted</span>
</pre>

:::

::: {.col .fragment}
## [**By human**]{.darkgreen}

### Plain text means the edit is a **diff**

<pre class="specimen diffcard">
<span>  ## EV Sales</span>
<span> </span>
<span>  Sales of **electric vehicles** grew 20% in 2025,</span>
<span class="sp-del">- reaching <span class="w">over</span> _20 million_ sales globally.</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ reaching <span class="w">nearly</span> _20 million_ sales globally.</span>
</pre>

:::

::: {.notes}
By machine: `quarto render` is a compile step, and an assertion can
fail the build.

By human: plain text means the edit is a diff. Review scales with the change,
not with the document.
:::

---

## [HTML is good, but it can't tell you if it's broken]{.center}

::: {.col .fragment}
[**HTML** - _manual_ numbers]{.red}

::: {.font140}
<pre class="specimen diffcard compact">
<span>  &lt;!DOCTYPE html&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;html lang="en"&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;head&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;meta charset="utf-8"&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;title&gt;EV Sales&lt;/title&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;style&gt;</span>
<span>  body { font-family: Georgia, serif;</span>
<span>         max-width: 40em; margin: 3em auto; }</span>
<span>  h2 { font-size: 1.6em; }</span>
<span>  &lt;/style&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;/head&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;body&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;h2&gt;EV Sales&lt;/h2&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;p&gt;Sales of &lt;strong&gt;electric vehicles&lt;/strong&gt; grew</span>
<span class="sp-del">- 20% in 2025, reaching over &lt;em&gt;<span class="w">18 million</span>&lt;/em&gt;</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ 20% in 2025, reaching over &lt;em&gt;<span class="w">20 million</span>&lt;/em&gt;</span>
<span>  sales globally.&lt;/p&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;/body&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;/html&gt;</span>
</pre>
:::

:::

::: {.col .fragment}
[**`.qmd`** - _computed_ numbers]{.blue}

::: {.font140}
<pre class="specimen diffcard compact">
<span>  ## EV Sales</span>
<span> </span>
<span>  Sales of **electric vehicles** grew</span>
<span>  20% in 2025, reaching over</span>
<span class="sp-del">- _<span class="w">20 million</span>_ sales globally.</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ _<span class="w">&#96;r ev_sales&#96; million</span>_ sales globally.</span>
</pre>
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Why not just ask for HTML? Agents are very good at it.

Because malformed HTML still renders as *something*, so the agent can't tell
whether it succeeded.

Left: nineteen lines, and the changed row has somewhere to hide. Right: compute
it once and never re-type it.
:::

# [What about interactivity?]{.font150}

---

`r rungbar(1)`

## Interactivity you get from a code chunk

::: {.col width="46%"}
[**Python**]{.blue}

::: {.font40}
```python
px.scatter(
  penguins,
  x = "bill_length_mm",
  y = "flipper_length_mm",
  color = "species"
)
```
:::

[**R**]{.blue}

::: {.font40}
```r
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  e_charts(bill_length_mm) |>
  e_scatter(flipper_length_mm)
```
:::

[Hover. Click the legend. &rarr;]{.font110}

[No input. No server. No reactive.]{.font110 .blue}
:::

::: {.col width="54%"}
```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
library(echarts4r)

penguins |>
  tidyr::drop_na(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, species) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  e_charts(bill_length_mm, height = "400px") |>
  e_scatter(flipper_length_mm, symbol_size = 9) |>
  e_color(c("#00798c", "#A77400", "#d1495b")) |>
  e_legend(bottom = 0, textStyle = list(fontSize = 16)) |>
  e_tooltip() |>
  e_x_axis(name = "Bill length (mm)") |>
  e_y_axis(
    name = "Flipper length (mm)",
    nameLocation = "middle",
    nameGap = 45
  ) |>
  e_grid(left = 80, right = 30, top = 20, bottom = 80)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Open the section here -- it doesn't need a divider of its own:

*"I promised I'd come back to this. Everything I've shown you was generated
before anyone opened it. So: what about the part where the user does something?"*

Then the ladder starts at the bottom. A plotting package that emits JavaScript --
plotly, echarts4r, highcharter, take your pick -- gives you hovering, tooltips
and legend filtering for the price of a code chunk.

Point at the two code blocks: **Python on top, R underneath, same document.**
Quarto doesn't care which one you're in. That's worth ten seconds at this
conference and no more.

Then the live chart: click a species out of the legend. No input, no server, no
reactive.

Don't say "rung one" or "step one" out loud. The bar does that job -- let the
room notice it on its own. The only thing worth pointing at, once, is the split
between the two group headers, and the right moment for that is slide 4.

NOTE: the Python block is deliberately static. Rendering it live means adding
`jupyter:` to the YAML and a working Python env on stage, for a chart that makes
exactly the same point as the R one. Don't make conference wifi a dependency.
:::

`r rungbar(2)`

## [Widgets that talk to each other: `crosstalk`]{.center}

```{r}
library(crosstalk)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

pen <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  tidyr::drop_na(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, species)
shared <- SharedData$new(pen)

htmltools::div(
  filter_slider("mass", "Body mass (g)", shared, ~body_mass_g, width = "100%"),
  htmltools::div(
    style = "display:flex; gap:1.2rem; margin-top:0.6rem;",
    htmltools::div(
      style = "flex:1 1 55%;",
      plot_ly(
        shared,
        x = ~bill_length_mm,
        y = ~flipper_length_mm,
        color = ~species,
        colors = c("#00798c", "#A77400", "#d1495b"),
        type = "scatter",
        mode = "markers",
        height = 290
      ) |>
        layout(showlegend = FALSE, margin = list(l = 45, r = 5, t = 5, b = 40))
    ),
    htmltools::div(
      style = "flex:1 1 45%;",
      datatable(
        shared,
        rownames = FALSE,
        options = list(pageLength = 5, dom = "t")
      )
    )
  )
)
```

[Move the slider. Drag a box on the plot. **Still no server.**]{.font120 .blue}

::: {.notes}
The obvious next question: *can one widget change another one?*

Yes -- `crosstalk`. Wrap the data frame in `SharedData$new()`, hand that to both
widgets instead of the data, and they're linked. Move the slider and both
respond. Drag a box on the scatter and the table follows.

All of it in the browser. Still a static file.

**Say the limits before anyone asks -- this audience will know them:**
widget authors have to opt in, so it's plotly, leaflet, DT, reactable, not
everything. Notably **not echarts4r**, which is why this demo isn't from my
site. And it filters *rows*, not aggregates -- it can hide points, it can't
recompute a regression.

That's the honest ceiling, and it's exactly what the next slide climbs over.
:::

---

`r rungbar(2)`

## [Or recompute in the browser: `ojs`]{.center}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ojs_define(
  pen_ojs = palmerpenguins::penguins |>
    tidyr::drop_na(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, species) |>
    dplyr::select(species, bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)
)
```

::: {.col width="38%"}
::: {.font40}
````markdown
```{r}
ojs_define(pen_ojs = penguins)
```

```{ojs}
data = transpose(pen_ojs)
viewof mass = Inputs.range(
  [2700, 6300], {label: "Min mass"})
```
````
:::

[R hands the data over.<br>The browser does the rest.]{.font110 .blue}

[This one **recomputes** -- the fit is<br>refitted client-side, not filtered.]{.font110}
:::

::: {.col width="62%"}
```{ojs}
data = transpose(pen_ojs)

viewof mass = Inputs.range([2700, 6300], {step: 50, value: 2700, label: "Min mass (g)"})

filtered = data.filter(d => d.body_mass_g >= mass)

Plot.plot({
  height: 320,
  marginLeft: 55,
  color: {domain: ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"],
          range: ["#00798c", "#A77400", "#d1495b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(filtered, {x: "bill_length_mm", y: "flipper_length_mm",
                        fill: "species", r: 4, fillOpacity: 0.75}),
    Plot.linearRegressionY(filtered, {x: "bill_length_mm",
                                      y: "flipper_length_mm", stroke: "#2e4057"})
  ]
})
```
:::

::: {.notes}
And if filtering isn't enough -- if you need it to actually *compute* -- Quarto
ships Observable JS.

`ojs_define()` hands an R data frame to the browser. From there it's a reactive
runtime: change the input, everything downstream re-evaluates.

**Point at the regression line.** That's the difference from the last slide.
Crosstalk hides points. This refits the line as you move the slider. Nobody
called a server, and there's no R running anywhere -- the page has been static
this whole time.

Don't oversell. OJS is JavaScript, so this is where an R-only room hits a
language boundary -- and that's a fair reason to reach for Shiny two rungs up.
Say it plainly; it makes rung 4 land better.
:::

[Six lines. That's the **entire** interface between the page<br>and whatever is on the other end.]{.font130 .blue}

::: {.notes}
Everything so far lives inside the document. Here's where that stops.

**This is the one slide where the bar is worth a glance.** The colour changed,
and it changed here for a reason: everything to the left of that line is
something Quarto gives you. Everything to the right is something Quarto
*composes*.

The slide itself is six lines, and they are the entire contract between a Quarto
page and something that isn't one. The page says *where*. It never says *what*.

Fifteen seconds. Don't dwell -- it's a hinge, not a destination. The next two
slides are what it holds.

## [Yes, you can still use Shiny]{.center}

::: {.col}
[**Shinylive** -- no server]{.blue}

````markdown
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 800
```
````

Compiled to WebAssembly, running in the reader's browser. Two pages on my site
are exactly this.
:::

::: {.col}
[**A real Shiny server**]{.red}

::: {.font55}
```r
tags$iframe(
  src = "https://shiny.example.com/explorer",
  height = "700px", width = "100%"
)
```
:::

When WASM isn't enough -- a database, data too big to ship -- deploy it and
point at it.
:::

<br>

[Same six lines either way. **The page can't tell the difference.**]{.font130 .blue}

::: {.notes}
Be generous here. This is a Posit conference and Shiny is the right answer to a
real class of problem: server-side compute over data too big for a browser,
live connections, anything that has to reach a database. I am not arguing
against Shiny.

I'm arguing that the *page* doesn't need to know. Shinylive if it fits in the
browser; a deployed app if it doesn't. Same iframe.

And that's the one thing in this entire talk that costs money -- and it costs it
inside one rectangle instead of across the whole site.

NOTE: the right-hand example is generic. If you don't have a deployed app, say
"if you needed one." Don't imply vehicletrends.us has a backend it doesn't have.
:::

::: {.notes}
Top of the ladder. No package did this. It's hand-written MapLibre against 1.64
GB of vector tiles on a CDN, and it is the hardest thing on the entire site.

Which is exactly why it isn't *in* the site. It's its own repo, and it was its
own conversation -- **the agent that built this never saw the dashboard, and the
dashboard has never seen these 276 lines.**

Six lines is everything they know about each other.

That's the agent argument from the cost section showing up as architecture, and
it's the reason this rung sits above Shiny rather than below it: the ladder is
ordered by how much you have to *build*, not how much infrastructure you need.
:::

## [The page says *where*. It never says *what*.]{.center}

<br>

::: {.col}
[**inside the document**]{.blue}

1. a **JS widget** -- hover, legend, tooltip
2. **crosstalk** or **ojs** -- linked, or recomputed
:::

::: {.col}
[**in a box**]{.red}

3. an **iframe** -- six lines
4. **Shiny** -- WASM, or a real server
5. **anything** -- 276 lines of MapLibre
:::

<br>

[Five kinds of interactive. One kind of hole in the page.]{.font130}

[The document can't tell them apart. Neither can the agent.]{.font130 .blue}

::: {.notes}
No bar on this slide, deliberately -- the bar has been the map, and this is the
territory. Same two group labels, same two colours, now unpacked.

Five kinds of interactivity, and the document treats every one of them the same
way: it says where the thing is, and nothing about what it is.

That's the whole architecture. Every box was built alone, in its own repo, in
its own conversation -- and every one is six lines to the page that holds it.

**The agent line is the point of the slide, not a flourish.** The agent inherits
exactly the ignorance the page has. It works on one box at a time and never
needs the system in its head.

No fragments here. They've just seen all five -- this is a recap, not a reveal.
:::

## It's just static files

Everything here runs in the browser, and the whole site is files — **hosted for free.**

- charts → ECharts (JS), rendered client-side
- the map → PMTiles on a CDN, instant
- the Shiny app → **Shinylive**, compiled to WebAssembly. No server.

A GitHub Action re-renders and republishes it **every Sunday at 5am.** Nothing is
cached, so nothing goes stale.

[No server to run. No server to secure. No server to pay for.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
Say "static files," not "serverless" — serverless drags in Lambda and edge
functions and backends. This is simpler than that.

At the end of the day it's a folder of files a browser can read. So I can host
it for free.

If you kept the correctness-at-scale slide, the Sunday re-render is already
spent. Drop that sentence here and let this slide be purely about hosting.

## You don't need to know Quarto to get started

Change **one word** in your prompt.

[Ask for the `.qmd`.]{.font160 .blue}

## Where this gets annoying

- agents invent chunk options that don't exist — `quarto render` catches it, but only if you make them run it
- Quarto's errors point at the **rendered** line, not always the line you wrote
- a big render loop is slow; cache it or the agent will wait, and so will you
- models still write 2023-era Quarto — expect `output:` where you wanted `format:`

[None of these are fatal. All of them are cheaper than re-prompting a PDF.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
NEW SLIDE — RECOMMENDED. Edit the four bullets down to whatever actually bit
you; the specific gripes matter less than the fact that you have some.

This buys credibility with the skeptic in row three, and it makes the next
slide read as mitigation rather than boilerplate. A talk that admits nothing
gets argued with in the hallway.

Keep it fast — twenty seconds, no dwelling. The last line is the whole point of
the slide.
:::

---

## Make this work Monday

1. Put *"always run `quarto render` before finishing"* in your `CLAUDE.md`
2. Have the agent work on a branch, so edits arrive as diffs
3. Keep data in files the `.qmd` reads — never in the prompt

::: {.notes}
Three things you can do Monday.

Read them fast. If you added the caveats slide before this one, these three now
read as mitigations, which is a better register than advice.
:::

## It's  application. It's a document.

::: {.col}
[**Shiny**]{.red}

- a UI
- a server function
- a reactive graph
- a process that has to be running

You maintain an **application**.
:::

::: {.col}
[**Quarto**]{.blue}

- markdown
- a chunk that returns a widget

You maintain a **document**.
:::

[No UI. No server. Real compute over data too big for a browser is still Shiny's job.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
This isn't an application. It's a document.

Not an anti-Shiny argument: real server-side compute over data too big for a
browser is exactly Shiny's job. Most dashboards aren't that.

This slide is early on purpose. This room has been silently asking "why isn't
